standard_text: Going on a nature trail: observing plants, birds and insects with care; using binoculars and a magnifying glass; beaks and toes of birds; insects and other small animals; recognising trees; signs of animals; behaving well in nature (summary of NCERT Our Wondrous World Chapter 3).

key_big: Observe quietly; leave nature as you found it.
key_sub: A bird's beak and toes suit its food and home.
body_html:
How to think about it

On a nature trail we walk slowly and quietly, using binoculars to watch birds and a magnifying glass to look at insects and leaves. We note footprints, feathers and nests, and we draw what we see in a nature diary. Insects have six legs and three body parts; spiders, with eight legs, are not insects.

Birds' beaks and toes suit their food and habits: an eagle has a hooked beak and talons, a duck a flat beak and webbed toes, a woodpecker a strong pointed beak and toes for climbing. We stay on the path, do not pluck flowers and take our litter home.

Example

A spider: insect or not?

count its legs

Answer: not an insect (eight legs)

Example

A flat, broad beak is for…

a duck's beak

Answer: straining food from water

Common mistakes

  • Calling a spider an insect.
  • Plucking flowers on a trail.
  • Thinking all birds have the same kind of toes.

faq.a: It has six legs and three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

faq.q: Why do birds have different beaks?
faq.a: Each beak suits the bird's food: hooked for meat, thin for nectar, strong and short for seeds.
